title: Surviving in the Desert
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: A desert is a region that receives less than about two hundred and fifty millimetres of rain a year. Deserts cover roughly a third of the Earth's land surface, and they are not all hot and sandy: some, like parts of Antarctica, are cold, and many are stony rather than sandy. Uzbekistan has its own, the Kyzylkum, whose name means red sand. Life in a desert seems impossible, yet thousands of species live there. They have solved the two great problems of the desert, which are the shortage of water and the extremes of temperature, in ways that are often ingenious. This passage describes four of these solutions and the lessons that they offer.

The camel is the most famous desert animal. Contrary to popular belief, its hump does not hold water but fat, which can be used as a store of energy when food is scarce. The camel's real secret is its ability to cope with thirst. It can lose a quarter of its body weight in water without serious harm, an amount that would kill most mammals, and when it finds a well it can drink more than a hundred litres in a few minutes. Its wide, flat feet spread its weight on soft sand, its thick eyelashes and closing nostrils keep out blowing dust, and its thick coat protects it from the heat.

The fennec fox, the smallest fox in the world, lives in the Sahara. Its enormous ears, which may be fifteen centimetres long, serve two purposes: they give the fox a sharp sense of hearing for finding insects underground, and they act like radiators, releasing heat from the blood vessels near the surface of the skin. The fox sleeps in a burrow during the heat of the day and hunts only at night, when the desert is cool. Its pale colour reflects the sunlight, and the thick fur on its feet protects them from the burning sand. It can survive with very little water, gaining most of what it needs from its food.

Some animals never drink at all. The kangaroo rat of the North American desert gets all its water from the seeds that it eats, and from the chemical processes in its own body. It loses very little: its kidneys produce a highly concentrated urine, its droppings are dry, and it spends the day in a cool, humid burrow, which it seals with earth. It does not sweat. Scientists have studied the animal closely to learn how it saves water, and some of their findings have been used in the design of equipment that recycles water in places where it is scarce.

Desert plants face the same problems. Cacti have swollen stems in which they store water, and their leaves have evolved into spines, which reduce the loss of water and protect against animals. Their roots spread wide just below the surface, so that they can absorb a brief shower before it evaporates. Other plants avoid the drought altogether. Their seeds lie in the sand for years, sometimes for decades, and germinate only when heavy rain falls. Within days, the plants flower, produce new seeds and die, so that a barren plain can turn into a carpet of colour for a few weeks, an event that attracts visitors from around the world.

A common solution is to avoid the day. Most desert animals are nocturnal, which means that they are active at night, when the temperature may be as much as thirty degrees lower than at midday. Insects, snakes, lizards and small mammals shelter underground or under rocks, where the temperature is much more stable. Even a few centimetres below the surface of the sand, the heat is far less severe. Some beetles collect drinking water from the morning fog by standing with their bodies tilted and letting the droplets run down to their mouths.

Dr Amir Nazarov, a desert ecologist, believes that humans can learn from these adaptations. Architects are copying the thick walls and shaded courtyards of desert towns, engineers are designing nets to catch water from fog, and farmers are testing crops that need little water. At the same time, he warns that deserts are growing. Overgrazing, the cutting of trees and the changing climate are turning dry grassland into desert, a process called desertification, which threatens the homes of hundreds of millions of people. The solution, he says, is to plant trees and protect the soil, before the land is lost.
